evidence_notes.reason: No full text retrieved; do not infer from abstract.

evidence_notes.research_design: Controlled synthetic Mars-rover decision-support benchmark: 100 labeled scenarios, five repeated runs per scenario and architecture, and two same-provider model backends (OpenAI GPT-4o and GPT-5.5). It compares one generalist call with a supervisor-style pipeline of telemetry, terrain, risk, and mission-planning specialists plus an orchestrator. Primary inference aggregates repetitions to 100 paired scenario-level units, uses exact paired sign tests, reports Cohen's dz with paired-scenario bootstrap confidence intervals, and applies Holm-Bonferroni correction across ten comparisons. GPT-4o-only one-role-at-a-time ablations use paired run-level McNemar tests.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Both conditions use the same synthetic scenarios, backend within each comparison, sanitized operational inputs, constrained JSON output fields, and evaluator-only expected-action/hazard labels; prompts, model-facing fields, schemas, and run metadata are documented. The single agent receives the complete scenario, while specialists receive role-relevant subsets and the orchestrator receives sanitized full context plus specialist outputs, so information partitioning and prompt/role design are inseparable from agent count. The multi-agent condition also necessarily makes five calls rather than one. The task is short-context, static, tool-less, and outside software development; there are no heterogeneous models, independent data/tool access, production deployment, or human-validated operational labels.
headline_results: GPT-4o single versus multi: decision accuracy 0.810 versus 0.734; exact hazard F1 0.081 versus 0.043; semantic hazard F1 0.131 versus 0.106; mean latency 2.32 s versus 11.83 s; mean tokens 458 versus 2,273.

GPT-5.5 single versus multi: decision accuracy 0.974 versus 0.934; exact hazard F1 0.018 versus 0.000; semantic hazard F1 0.075 versus 0.060; mean latency 6.06 s versus 35.59 s; mean tokens 548 versus 3,160.

After scenario-level aggregation and Holm correction, neither decision-accuracy difference was significant (GPT-4o adjusted p = 0.087; GPT-5.5 adjusted p = 0.238). The sole corrected decision-quality difference was GPT-5.5 exact hazard F1 (adjusted p = 0.001), despite very low absolute F1. Latency and token differences remained significant for both backends (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001).

Multi-agent orchestration increased mean false-positive hazards: 5.514 versus 1.526 for GPT-4o and 6.084 versus 3.812 for GPT-5.5. It also increased canonical hazard coverage (0.214 versus 0.144 for GPT-4o; 0.127 versus 0.119 for GPT-5.5), but broader coverage included both plausible non-canonical and spurious hazards and lowered precision/F1.

GPT-4o ablations show unequal role value: removing terrain reduced multi-agent accuracy from 0.734 to 0.666 (p < 0.001), and removing mission planning reduced it to 0.684 (p = 0.003); removing telemetry (0.744, p = 0.551) or risk (0.758, p = 0.104) did not significantly hurt accuracy. Even the complete multi-agent pipeline remained below the single-agent baseline.
limitations: Synthetic labels encode a predefined policy and were not independently reviewed by rover operators, planetary scientists, or multiple annotators; exact and substring matching do not establish operational hazard relevance.
Only two OpenAI backends and one prompt-defined supervisor/aggregator design were tested; architecture is confounded with role prompts, context partitioning, call count, and arbitration logic.
The 100-scenario size and GPT-4o-only ablations were constrained by API cost and runtime; no dollar cost or energy use is reported.

No tools, separate data sources, long-horizon state, heterogeneous specialist models, real rover telemetry, flight hardware, or production workflow were evaluated, sharply limiting transfer to multi-agent software engineering.
Hazard-label fidelity was poor in every condition, so high action accuracy does not demonstrate reliable explanatory grounding.
future_work: Use larger corpora with human-annotated imagery, terrain-derived records, and independent expert review of actions and hazards.
Compare deterministic matching with expert annotation and richer semantic evaluation that separates canonical, plausible secondary, and unsupported hazards.
Test additional providers, domain-adapted models, heterogeneous and tool-using agents, alternative orchestration designs, and GPT-5.5 role ablations.
Evaluate explicit filtering, arbitration, evidence thresholds, and disagreement-resolution rules rather than union-like specialist aggregation.
combinable_methods: Use a single agent for compact fully contextualized tasks, escalating to multiple agents only when roles have genuinely distinct tools, data, modalities, or long-horizon work.
Add a critic/filter orchestrator with evidence requirements, confidence thresholds, and intersection-style agreement to suppress unsupported specialist claims.

Preserve evaluator-only labels, structured outputs, repeated matched scenarios, scenario-level paired inference, multiple-comparison correction, and role ablations as an architecture-evaluation protocol.
Separate primary hazards from secondary context and audit canonical coverage, plausible additions, spurious outputs, latency, and tokens jointly rather than optimizing aggregate task accuracy alone.

quotes.text: In the single-agent architecture, one generalized LLM agent receives the complete rover scenario context and independently generates a final operational recommendation. In the multi-agent orchestration architecture, specialized agents independently evaluate telemetry, terrain, risk, and mission-planning factors before forwarding intermediate outputs to an orchestration layer responsible for synthesizing the final recommendation.
quotes.use: Defines the matched architecture comparison and the role-specialized decomposition.

quotes.text: In the GPT-4o evaluation, the single-agent architecture achieved 0.810 decision accuracy, 0.081 exact hazard F1, and 0.131 semantic hazard F1. By comparison, GPT-4o multi-agent orchestration achieved 0.734 decision accuracy, 0.043 exact hazard F1, and 0.106 semantic hazard F1. The single-agent condition also required lower latency and token usage, averaging 2.32 s and 458 tokens per evaluation, compared with 11.83 s and 2,273 tokens for multi-agent orchestration.
quotes.use: Provides exact GPT-4o quality, latency, and token metrics.

quotes.text: Because the multi-agent condition necessarily required multiple specialist calls plus a final orchestration step for every scenario, the latency and token advantages of the single-agent architecture should be interpreted as an expected structural consequence of the tested design, with statistical testing quantifying the magnitude of that overhead rather than establishing it as an unexpected empirical discovery.
quotes.use: Qualifies the cost result as structural to the tested call topology.

quotes.text: The results therefore suggest that multi-agent orchestration may be most useful when the problem requires genuinely separable expertise, independent data access, tool execution, or long-horizon workflows that exceed the practical capabilities of a single model call.
quotes.use: States the paper's boundary conditions for when specialization may add value.

quotes.text: A different orchestrator design that acts more explicitly as a critic or filter, using confidence thresholds, evidence requirements, or intersection-style agreement rules, may reduce hazard inflation.
quotes.use: Identifies a complementary reliability mechanism for multi-agent aggregation.

evidence_notes.research_design: Non-peer-reviewed preprint evaluating five title/abstract-screening strategies: single model, three-model majority vote, recall-focused OR ensemble, self-confidence-weighted aggregation, and a fast-filter/two-model debate pipeline. Four locally hosted 4-bit 7-8B open-source models (Mistral 7B, LLaMA 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Granite 3.3 8B) were used in zero-shot and few-shot modes on a blockchain e-voting corpus. Ground truth was 200 keyword-enriched records independently screened by two humans and adjudicated on 50 disagreements; observed agreement was 75.0%, Cohen's kappa 0.515, and PABAK 0.500. Ten error-selected calibration papers were excluded from few-shot evaluation, leaving 190 records. Twenty-five completed/non-degenerate configurations were reported after three of 28 planned configurations were excluded.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Strategies receive the same title/abstract fields, domain criteria, human labels, local Apple-MLX deployment class, and 4-bit model scale; each model is also measured alone, and calibration examples are excluded from scored few-shot records. This is not a matched same-model/same-prompt/same-compute single-versus-multi experiment: ensemble arms combine heterogeneous models, use different aggregation prompts/rules and call counts, and the headline compares the best selected single configuration with the best selected ensemble after testing many combinations. Zero-shot uses N = 200 while few-shot uses N = 190. No repeated stochastic runs, paired architecture test, token totals, wall-clock latency, dollar/energy cost, or production use are reported. Full-corpus metrics are still calculated only on the same 190 embedded labeled records, leaving labels for additional selected records unknown.
headline_results: The best reported configuration was single-agent Qwen 2.5 7B few-shot: recall 100.0%, precision 70.4%, F1 82.6%, WSS@95 43.4%, with 69 TP, 29 FP, 0 FN, and 92 TN on N = 190. The best multi-agent configuration, two-stage Qwen to Mistral+LLaMA few-shot, obtained recall 100.0%, precision 61.6%, F1 76.2%, and WSS@95 36.0% (43 FP).

Qwen single-agent zero-shot had the highest zero-shot precision (72.9%) and F1 (82.3%) but missed the 95% recall threshold at 94.6% (4 FN); error-driven few-shot examples raised recall to 100.0% while precision fell to 70.4%.

Majority voting and confidence-weighted aggregation produced identical results for each tested ensemble, so self-reported HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW confidence added no discrimination. Recall-focused OR aggregation amplified false positives without a recall gain. Two-stage debate filtered up to 38.4% of records at stage 1, reported as an 18% inference saving, but did not improve precision.

Granite single-agent classified 199/200 zero-shot records as INCLUDE (126 FP, 0 TN; WSS@95 -4.5%) and retained 0 TN few-shot; this weakness propagated into ensembles, showing that adding a weak member can degrade aggregation.

The 95% Wilson precision intervals overlap across the top five configurations, and the authors state that N = 190 is insufficient to establish significant gaps. On the full 2,036-record corpus, single Qwen selected 950 records versus 1,131 for the best debate system; 926/950 single selections were common to all four top multi-agent systems, while the relevance of 140 multi-only selections was not full-text validated.
limitations: The application is one terminologically overloaded literature-screening domain, not software development, and the 200-record keyword-enriched gold standard is a stress-test sample rather than a representative corpus sample.

The top single-versus-multi comparison is a best-configuration ranking across different model mixtures and call budgets, not a controlled agent-count intervention with matched model, prompt, context, and compute.
Overlapping confidence intervals, no paired significance tests, and no repeated inference runs leave both superiority and nondeterministic stability unresolved.

Moderate human agreement (kappa 0.515) makes labels uncertain; results are not split between agreed and adjudicated cases. Error-driven few-shot examples came from the same corpus, which the authors identify as possible indirect leakage.

The claimed full-corpus stability re-scores only embedded gold-standard items; 140 papers selected by every top multi-agent configuration but not by the single agent were not adjudicated by full-text review.

Only quantized 7-8B models on consumer Apple hardware were evaluated. The paper reports a stage-call saving but no latency, tokens, monetary cost, energy use, or operational deployment evidence; a private chain provides provenance, not decision correctness.
future_work: Validate across domains with different terminology and larger models, including whether higher-capacity agents gain from deliberation.
Report results separately for human-agreed and adjudicated labels and increase sample size/power for paired strategy comparisons.
Use full-text retrieval-augmented generation to address title/abstract information limits and active learning to select informative records for human labeling.
Determine which inclusion/exclusion criteria contribute most and refine them without sacrificing discrimination.
combinable_methods: Perform domain-specific model selection and error-driven few-shot calibration before adding coordination; exclude calibration records from evaluation and test for corpus-level leakage.

When no single model meets a recall floor, use simple majority voting; use a two-stage gate only when measured call savings justify its precision tradeoff, and avoid self-confidence weighting without calibration evidence.
Keep humans in the loop through dual independent labeling, explicit uncertain decisions, third-reviewer resolution, and active-learning review of boundary cases.
Combine full-text RAG with explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria to resolve contribution type rather than relying on title/abstract keywords.
Preserve decision provenance with immutable operational logs, public timestamp anchoring, and archival artifacts, while evaluating correctness independently of audit integrity.

quotes.text: The best overall configuration was S1 with Qwen 2.5 7B (few-shot), which achieved perfect recall (100.0%), precision of 70.4%, F1 of 82.6%, and WSS@95 of 43.4%. This was the highest-ranked configuration across all 25 tested combinations.
quotes.use: Gives the exact best single-agent metrics and selection context.

quotes.text: Third, multi-agent strategies did not consistently outperform the single-agent baseline — the best S1 configuration surpassed all multi-agent alternatives. The 95% Wilson confidence intervals for precision overlapped across the top five configurations (Table 9), suggesting that the observed ranking differences may not be statistically robust at the current sample size.
quotes.use: Captures both the negative headline and its statistical qualification.

quotes.text: S2 (majority voting) and S4 (confidence-weighted aggregation) produced identical results across all metrics. This indicates that self-reported confidence from 7–8B parameter models does not add discriminative value.
quotes.use: Records the exact null result for self-confidence weighting.

quotes.text: S5 (two-stage debate) offered computational efficiency by filtering up to 38.4% of papers in Stage 1 (an 18% inference saving), but did not improve precision. S3 (recall-focused OR) amplified false positives without recall gains.
quotes.use: Provides the debate cost result and negative recall-ensemble result.

quotes.text: Future work should validate these findings across domains with different terminological characteristics and examine whether larger models benefit from multi-agent coordination. Two technical extensions could further address the persistent false positive pool: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) could provide full-text access during screening, and active learning could iteratively refine the decision boundary by selecting the most informative papers for human review.
quotes.use: Identifies complementary retrieval and human-labeling mechanisms.

evidence_notes.research_design: Technical note combining decision-theoretic results with controlled LLM mechanism experiments. It models an acyclic multi-agent workflow as a delegated decision network with shared context, optional node-private exogenous signals, endogenous finite-capacity messages, ancillary randomness, terminal action under bounded loss, and optional human recourse. It proves that a delegated network cannot beat a centralized Bayes decision maker observing all the same exogenous signals; in the common-evidence regime, graph optimization reduces to choosing a budget-constrained stochastic encoder. Under proper scoring rules, communication loss equals expected posterior divergence (conditional mutual information for log loss and squared posterior error for Brier loss). Empirically, it uses 200 balanced four-choice MMLU questions with GPT-4.1-mini and o4-mini across centralized, 2/3/5-stage relay, structured-posterior relay, Wikipedia/tool, and specialist conditions, plus 200 synthetic knowledge-base questions requiring lookup. Main conditions nominally use 30 runs/question and added conditions 10, although reported run totals vary.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Within relay-depth tests the backend and MMLU questions are shared, no new external signals are added, and downstream stages receive only the preceding relay; the structured-interface comparison keeps three stages fixed while changing prose to a four-class probability vector. Tool tests distinguish redundant MMLU retrieval from a synthetic task whose fabricated facts require lookup. These are mechanism checks, not a matched production single-versus-specialized comparison: the relay deliberately removes the original question from downstream agents, so terminal context capacity is not equal to the centralized baseline; the structured comparison is reported on only 50 questions; tool/specialist conditions change exogenous information; and the paper itself says MMLU is not a planning benchmark. It evaluates neither software development nor production workflows and reports no latency, token, energy, or human-review experiment.
headline_results: The formal ceiling is conditional: without new exogenous signals, internal messages and randomization cannot improve on a centralized Bayes decision maker with all available signals. In common-evidence serial chains, each communication step contributes nonnegative information loss under log loss unless it preserves the relevant posterior.

GPT-4.1-mini MMLU accuracy fell from 90.7% centralized to 41.2% with a two-stage prose relay, 43.5% with three stages, and 22.5% with five stages; o4-mini fell from 89.9% centralized to 37.0% with three stages. The five-stage result is below the 25% chance level, but downstream relay agents were intentionally denied the original question.

On a 50-question subset with the same three-stage depth, a posterior-vector relay reached 75.2% versus 58.1% for free-form prose; reported degradation was about 2.8 versus 8.5 percentage points per stage. Per-question proxy KL distortion correlated with accuracy loss at r = 0.72 for the three-agent prose condition and r = 0.44 for five agents, but model token distributions are explicitly not literal Bayesian posteriors.

Wikipedia did not improve the aggregate GPT-4.1-mini MMLU table result (87.2% with Wikipedia versus 90.7% centralized), while the synthetic knowledge-base tool raised accuracy from 24.3% to 82.7% (+58.4 points), supporting the distinction between redundant processing and genuinely new signal.

A nonredundant verifier signal can strictly improve Bayes value, whereas self-critique that only re-reads the terminal state cannot. Optimal human escalation compares automated posterior risk with conditional review loss case by case, rather than triggering on role count or disagreement alone.
limitations: The dominance result compares a real delegated policy to an ideal centralized Bayes decision maker, not necessarily to an implemented single LLM; it assumes fixed exogenous information, known loss, acyclic finite workflows, conditionally independent ancillary randomness, and (for the encoder result) common evidence and finite terminal-message cardinality.

The theory does not say all multi-agent systems are inferior: private signals, executable feedback, databases, environment observations, and nonredundant review change the information structure and can add value.

The central empirical relay comparison forces downstream stages to lose direct access to the question. It therefore demonstrates communication garbling under an unequal terminal context, not an agent-count effect under matched prompts, information, tools, and context budget.

MMLU multiple choice is not planning or software engineering; the synthetic lookup task is a mechanism check. There is no long-horizon execution, role-specialized SDLC task, human-review trial, security analysis, or production evidence.

Run totals and labels are not fully uniform (for example, 5,973 centralized GPT-4.1-mini runs, 5,138 three-relay runs, and a 50-question structured-relay subset), and the paper reports approximate API spend of $70 plus $15-25 but no per-condition latency, tokens, or energy.
The posterior analysis uses answer-token probabilities as operational proxies, and the authors explicitly state they are not formal Bayesian posteriors.
future_work: Develop communication-constrained planning methods that optimize decision-relevant information preservation rather than role or round count.
Study tool-mediated decision support where stages acquire genuinely new signals and separate those gains from delegation effects.
Build human-AI systems with structured recourse based on terminal posterior risk and review cost.
Evaluate architectures with matched exogenous signals and matched terminal-state capacity, using posterior distortion rather than transcript length as the communication-quality measure.
combinable_methods: Give specialized agents nonredundant executable tests, external validators, environment observations, database lookups, or distinct retrieval sources; do not count repeated self-critique over the same transcript as new evidence.
Use structured, typed handoffs that preserve calibrated decision state (for example, class posteriors) instead of unconstrained prose summaries, and measure handoff-induced posterior distortion.
Retain a centralized full-information baseline and match exogenous signals plus terminal communication capacity when attributing gains to architecture.
Escalate to humans when estimated automated posterior risk exceeds conditional review loss, rather than using fixed rounds, disagreement alone, or blanket review.
Separate information acquisition, communication, and recourse in both design and evaluation so reliability gains are credited to the mechanism that caused them.

quotes.text: Accordingly, a clean evaluation of multi-agent planning should compare architectures under matched exogenous signals and matched terminal state capacity, and should treat any additional retrieval, tool output, or larger shared workspace as a change in information structure rather than as a pure architecture effect.
quotes.use: States the required controls for attributing a gain to multi-agent architecture.

quotes.text: In particular, self-critique that only re-reads M cannot move the Bayes envelope, but executable tests or external validators can.
quotes.use: Distinguishes redundant reflection from verification that adds evidence.

quotes.text: On gpt-4.1-mini, accuracy falls from 90.7% in (A) to 41.2% in (B2), 43.5% in (B), and 22.5% in (B5). On o4-mini, the analogous drop from (A) to (B) is from 89.9% to 37.0%.
quotes.use: Provides exact centralized-versus-relay accuracy figures.

quotes.text: On the synthetic task in condition (S), accuracy rises from 24.3% without the tool to 82.7% with tool access. This pattern is consistent with Corollary 9, which predicts gains when an added signal contributes genuinely new information.
quotes.use: Shows the large gain when a tool supplies indispensable exogenous information.

quotes.text: In the relay conditions, downstream stages see only the relayed message and not the original question. This restriction is important because in this way, any change in performance then comes from the information passed through the workflow rather than from repeated direct access to the source problem. Total API cost is approximately $70 for the original conditions and $15-25 for the additional conditions.
quotes.use: Exposes the deliberate context restriction and the only reported cost figure.

evidence_notes.research_design: Proof-of-concept evaluation of transparent middleware placed between a client and the official GitHub MCP server, targeting the microsoft/vscode repository with read-only authentication. The research team authored 120 queries: 20 explicit-ID, 50 semantic, 20 context-reference, 20 adversarial, and 10 mixed. The named Executor, Validator, and Refiner are deterministic modules using regex intent parsing, rule/schema and similarity checks, ranking, session-scoped state, and clarification; core validation requires no LLM, although OpenAI text-embedding-3-small supplies 1,536-dimensional embeddings for semantic ranking. Outcomes are correct, disambiguation, or hallucination, with category-specific ground truth. Direct MCP, embedding-ranked RAG, and GPT-4o parsing baselines are architecturally described on the same server/repository, but their hallucination rates are not measured.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The alternatives are characterized against the same 120 author-designed queries, repository, official MCP stack, and base API latency. Direct MCP returns the first result, RAG returns the top embedding-ranked result, GPT-4o (temperature 0.3) constructs a call, and the proposed middleware validates or asks. However, the paper explicitly says a direct numerical comparison is impossible because semantic queries lack user-provided intended-item ground truth; Table III compares capabilities, not measured baseline errors. It is not a matched single-LLM versus multi-LLM study: the proposed 'agents' are deterministic Python components, baselines omit disambiguation/context by construction, and query handling plus compute differ. The benchmark uses production server code and a live public repository, but not production users, independently sampled logs, multiple backends, or a deployed enterprise workload.
headline_results: Under the paper's definition, the middleware produced 0 confident wrong items in 120 trials and all 50 semantic queries triggered clarification. This measures ambiguity detection, not eventual retrieval of the user's intended item; the paper says that end-to-end semantic retrieval requires a user study with intent labels.

Overall pattern coverage was 52% (62/120 rounded), comprising 43% disambiguation and 8% exact-match success. The remaining 48% were not parsed and passed through without validation benefit. Per-category coverage was explicit ID 25%, semantic 100%, context 5%, adversarial 0%, and mixed 60%.

Observed hallucinations were zero, but the paper reports a rule-of-three 95% upper bound of approximately 2.5% for the true rate; the small author-designed sample cannot establish rare-failure reliability.

Mean end-to-end latency was 2,322 ms and reported local validation overhead was 2 ms (0.09%), with network/API time dominant. The system also calls text-embedding-3-small for semantic ranking, but no separate embedding latency, token, dollar, or energy cost is reported.

The reliability mechanism is conservative abstention: multiple matches yield a top-five shortlist and user clarification; malformed, unverifiable, absent, or unparsed cases return warnings/errors rather than a confident item. Deterministic core logic makes repeated outputs stable against a fixed repository snapshot, with repository evolution identified as the remaining nondeterminism.
limitations: No baseline error, success, latency distribution, or statistical comparison is measured; the claimed contrast is architectural because intended-item ground truth is absent for ambiguous searches.
Calling deterministic regex, rules, and ranking components 'agents' does not test whether specialized LLM agents outperform one LLM under matched models, prompts, tools, or compute.

Semantic success is defined as requesting clarification, adversarial success permits rejection/pass-through, and 48% of all patterns receive no validation benefit; thus 0% hallucination does not mean 100% task completion or coverage.

Queries are author-designed and all English; one public GitHub repository and one MCP backend limit external validity. Adversarial coverage is 0%, and attacks such as prompt injection, authorization bypass, data leakage, or malicious tool responses are not evaluated.
Zero events in 120 trials leave an approximately 2.5% upper confidence bound. No user study confirms that shortlists contain intended items or quantifies clarification burden and productivity.

The 2 ms figure applies to local deterministic validation while semantic ranking uses an embedding API; the paper provides no isolated embedding latency/cost, throughput, tail latency, operational monitoring, or production deployment evidence.
future_work: Evaluate Jira, Azure DevOps, and other MCP backends with adapter-specific schemas and identifiers.
Use larger, independently constructed or user-generated multilingual query sets across multiple repositories and organizations.
Conduct user studies with ground-truth intent to measure eventual retrieval success, clarification burden, and productivity.
Expand query-pattern and adversarial coverage and test richer context tracking across sessions.
combinable_methods: Place deterministic validation middleware around LLM tool calls: parse explicit identifiers, validate existence/schema/type, ground relevance, and reject unverifiable outputs before user exposure.
Convert ambiguity into a bounded human choice by presenting a concise ranked shortlist and requiring clarification rather than allowing a confident single-result guess.
Maintain explicit session-scoped query, result, mention, and disambiguation state for follow-up references, with clear reset boundaries rather than implicit long-term memory.
Use conservative abstention and structured error states for unparsed, malformed, zero-result, and ambiguous requests; track coverage and completion separately from hallucination rate.
Run with least-privilege read-only tool credentials and validate independently sampled user-intent benchmarks before production deployment.

quotes.text: Core System: Our validation middleware uses a deterministic multi-agent architecture. The Executor uses regex-based parsing for query understanding. The Validator uses rule-based checks for response validation. The Refiner uses a ranking algorithm for disambiguation. No LLM is required for the core validation logic.
quotes.use: Establishes that the specialized 'agents' are deterministic modules, not LLM agents.

quotes.text: For semantic and context queries, correct behavior is requesting clarification (disambiguation), since no single item is objectively correct when hundreds match—the absence of a confident single return is the desired outcome.
quotes.use: Defines the ground truth behind the reported semantic success.

quotes.text: The remaining 48% of queries were not parsed by the system's regex library and were passed through to the MCP server without validation. While these cases produced no hallucinations (the system fails safely by design), they also provided no validation benefit.
quotes.use: Qualifies the zero-error result with the prototype's unvalidated coverage gap.

quotes.text: Because our validation agents are deterministic Python code (regex parsing, rule-based validation, ranking), the agent processing itself adds only 2ms of validation overhead while fundamentally changing the failure mode from 'confident wrong answer' to 'request for clarification.'
quotes.use: Provides the reported overhead and explains the abstention mechanism.

quotes.text: Because our system handles ambiguous queries through disambiguation rather than by returning a single item, direct apples-to-apples hallucination rate comparison with the baselines is not possible: the baselines return items that we cannot verify without user-provided ground truth.
quotes.use: States that the paper does not contain a measured comparative baseline.

evidence_notes.research_design: Master's thesis using a two-phase mixed-methods design. Phase 1 reviews 31 academic/grey sources from 2023-2026 and derives ten coordination patterns. Phase 2 compares a single agent, a sequential Planner-Coder-Tester pipeline, and a hierarchical Supervisor-Analyst/Writer topology on the same 30 self-contained Python TestEval tasks. Each architecture runs every task three times (90 executions/pattern; 270 total) with Claude Sonnet 4 through one AWS Bedrock endpoint, temperature 0.2, maxTokens 4,096, a nominal three-retry ceiling, local pytest/pytest-cov execution, and captured tokens, cost, latency, turns, coverage, errors, and traces. Analysis is descriptive (means, averaged within-run standard deviations/derived variances, CV, t-based 95% intervals, percentiles). Direct content analysis codes Run 1 traces for 22 tasks across all patterns (66 cases) using a prior frame and one coder.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The experiment matches foundation model, endpoint, inference parameters, 30 benchmark inputs, execution sandbox, measurement pipeline, three-run protocol, and nominal retry limit. It does not match literal prompts, context visibility, calls, or computational budget: each architecture has distinct unoptimized role prompts and control flow; the sequential system transfers planner artifacts, the hierarchy partitions context through a supervisor, and the single system lacks an intermediate planning role. Thus the intervention is the whole architecture package, including role prompts, information routing, verification timing, and number of calls. Equal lack of prompt optimization does not establish equal prompt quality, which the authors identify as an internal-validity threat. Repeated observations are naturally paired by task/run, but no paired hypothesis test or architecture effect size is reported; t intervals treat 90 execution records as the sample despite three repetitions of 30 tasks.
headline_results: Sequential achieved 92.2% success (83/90), 91.6% line coverage, 90.6% branch coverage, and 83% cross-run consistency (25/30 tasks). Single-agent achieved 81.1% (73/90), 80.6% line, 79.7% branch, and 67% consistency (20/30). Hierarchical achieved 54.4% (49/90), about 54% coverage, and 47% consistency (14/30). No paired statistical test establishes uncertainty on the 11.1-point sequential advantage.

Median latency was 35.05 s single (IQR 22.20-59.47), 41.52 s sequential (35.09-54.83), and 142.37 s hierarchical (114.72-185.22). Latency variance was reported as 603.29, 295.56, and 3,353.04 s^2 respectively; hierarchical p95 was 281.41 s versus 73.10 s sequential.

Mean cost/task was $0.083 single, $0.089 sequential, and $0.308 hierarchical; median turns were about 3, 4, and 10. Sequential averaged 11,507 tokens/task, only 17% above single in the qualitative section; the conclusion summarizes sequential as 1.2x single-agent token cost for +11.1 pass-rate points and hierarchical as 4.6x token cost for -26.7 points. Costs exclude infrastructure and human oversight.

Sequential planner specifications included explicit inputs, expected outputs, and code-path targets in 87/90 runs. In the 22-task trace sample, productive specialization appeared in 18 sequential cases and plan-guided generation in 3; this proactive artifact preceded code and reduced reliance on post-hoc retry. Single-agent traces showed iterative self-correction in 16/22 and assertion hallucination in 6/22; reported pass rate was 100% at 0-2 retries but 39% among cases reaching three retries.

Hierarchical traces showed productive specialization in 12/22 sampled cases and supervisor information bottlenecks in the other 10. Across all 41 hierarchical failures, no direct worker-to-worker information flow was observed: correct analyst reasoning was repeatedly re-requested but not delivered to the writer. On one task this consumed 43,957 tokens, 5.7x sequential, and failed all three runs. Hierarchy also uniquely produced 11 delegation-leak outputs exposing internal coordination instructions.

The thesis reports inconsistent test-failure summaries: per-run-average values of 1.89% single, 0.46% sequential, and 6.41% hierarchical, but a separate figure/discussion reports 2.83%, 1.41%, and 28.54%. It does not reconcile the denominators. Methods call the outcome pass@1 while trace examples count convergence after retries, leaving first-attempt versus final-retry success ambiguous.
limitations: One model, one 30-task sample, one benchmark family, one programming language, and one generation-oriented SE task do not establish a general architecture principle or end-to-end SDLC performance.

TestEval consists of public LeetCode-derived algorithms likely present in training data; the authors require replication on novel functions or private repositories before transfer to real-world test generation.

Only three stochastic runs may not characterize nondeterminism. No paired test, multiple-comparison treatment, power analysis, or task-cluster-aware interval is reported, and the unusual variance calculation squares the average of within-run standard deviations.

All prompts were standardized but unoptimized; architecture-specific prompt sensitivity may explain part of the gap. Roles, context partitions, message artifacts, calls, and feedback paths differ, so the experiment does not match prompts/tools/compute in the strict sense.

The meaning of success/pass@1 and test-failure rate is internally ambiguous, test-failure summaries conflict, and self-consistency with generated tests does not measure defect detection, mutation score, hidden-test adequacy, execution recovery, or resilience to unforeseen failures.

Qualitative analysis uses 22 purposively selected Run 1 traces, a prior coding frame, and one coder with no inter-rater reliability. The supervisor-bottleneck explanation is plausible trace evidence, not a causal mediation test.

The lab intentionally removes production context. Cost is token-price only, latency is exposed to API fluctuation, and there is no infrastructure, human-review, energy, throughput, concurrency, long-horizon repository, maintenance, security, or production deployment evaluation.
Sandboxing protects the experiment from generated code, but security is not evaluated; the 11 hierarchical delegation leaks indicate an output-boundary risk rather than a complete threat assessment.
future_work: Replicate the identical tasks, prompt configurations, and measures with another model such as Mistral Large, GPT-4o, or Llama 3 to test whether the supervisor bottleneck is model-specific.
Extend the matched comparison to requirements engineering, architecture design, bug repair, code review, and other SDLC phases with different interdependence structures.
Compare unoptimized and optimized prompts with equal optimization effort for each architecture to separate prompt sensitivity from architecture effects.
Use more runs, novel/private code, task-paired statistical analysis, independent qualitative coders, and richer measures of generated-test quality and execution-level recovery.
Test direct worker channels/shared workspaces and human-supervisor variants as remedies for supervisor-mediated information loss.
combinable_methods: For derivable test specifications, use a bounded sequential Planner-Coder-Tester pipeline whose planner emits a reviewable artifact containing explicit inputs, expected values, target paths, requirements, and constraints before code generation.

Execute generated tests in an isolated sandbox and feed deterministic failures back through bounded retries; distinguish proactive plan verification from post-hoc self-correction and record first-attempt separately from final-retry success.

Preserve full artifacts across handoffs. For hierarchy, add direct worker-to-worker channels or a typed shared workspace so correct analysis reaches the writer without supervisor summarization/re-delegation.
Expose intermediate plans, analyses, and draft tests to developers; place human review before code generation or use a human supervisor to audit business and security requirements.

Choose topology by task structure: single agent for short bounded work, sequential for work with an upfront derivable specification, and hierarchy only for independent decomposable subtasks; monitor pass rate, cross-run consistency, retries, turns, tokens, cost, latency tails, information routing, and delegation leakage together.

quotes.text: The hierarchical pattern suffered from supervisor information bottleneck according to the qualitative results confirmed by 100% of the failing tasks of the architecture. These results come from a single LLM, a single benchmark, and non-optimized prompts per architecture, which means replication is needed before these findings are treated as general architectural principles.
quotes.use: States the proposed hierarchy failure mechanism and the thesis's main scope qualification.

evidence_notes.research_design: Eight-page ASE workshop study over 673 multiple-choice prompts from PythonIO (127 algorithmic/programming prompts), LogiQA (283 logic prompts), and AGIEval (263 general exam prompts). It tests GPT-4o (A), Claude Sonnet (B), and Gemini 2.5 Pro (C) individually, then eight selected homogeneous/heterogeneous ordered Planner-Executor-Critic triples (AAA, ABC, BAB, BBB, BCC, CBA, CCA, CCC). Each triple has a simple relay condition and an accountable condition with structured handoffs, stagewise records, and offline blame attribution against gold labels. It reports final accuracy, median input/output tokens, provider-price-derived cost, end-to-end latency, planner error, executor/critic repair and harm, and configuration Pareto fronts. No repeated-run or inferential protocol is reported.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Simple and accountable pipelines use the same benchmark records and ordered model triple, making their within-row accuracy delta the cleanest comparison. Single-model baselines use the same answer space and datasets. However, accountable versus simple changes the handoff prompts/format and validation protocol, not just logging; multi-agent versus monolithic changes calls, context, roles, and compute. Heterogeneous pipelines also change model composition, while homogeneous AAA/BBB/CCC use three calls from one model versus one monolithic call. No tool access, requirements, open-ended code artifact, repeated sampling, matched token budget, temperature, confidence interval, paired significance test, or correction for selecting the best of eight configurations is reported. Gold labels enable blame after every stage offline but would not normally be available at runtime.
headline_results: Best monolithic Gemini accuracy was 92.40% on AGIEval (median 11.84 s, $0.0112/prompt), 99.21% on PythonIO (11.20 s, $0.0120), and 84.45% on LogiQA (14.78 s, $0.0134). By Table III, the best accountable pipeline reached 93.54%, 99.21%, and 85.16%, respectively: +1.14 points, a tie, and +0.71 versus the best single model, without uncertainty estimates.

Accountable versus simple versions of the same triple produced large but configuration-dependent gains: PythonIO BBB rose 61.42% to 97.64% (+36.22), BAB +33.07, CBA +27.56, and CCA +26.78; AGIEval AAA gained +19.78. Negative/null results remain: AGIEval BAB -2.28 and BCC -0.76; PythonIO BCC -0.78 and ABC/CCC 0; LogiQA AAA -0.10 and BBB -0.07.

Planner errors were strongly model/task dependent: Gemini 0.79-15.19%, Claude 3.94-22.03%, and GPT-4o 11.02-40.49% across datasets. Aggregated midstream profiles differed: Gemini executor/critic repair 1.27%/2.66% with 0.25% harm in both; Claude executor repair 10.01% with 0.25% harm but critic harm 1.90%; GPT-4o critic repair 5.20% and executor harm 1.33%. The authors recommend CBA casting (Gemini planner, Claude executor, GPT-4o critic).

Accountable pipelines cost about 2-3x monolithic baselines and increased median latency from about 2 s in lightweight settings to 20-25 s in heavier settings (about 8-10x). Pareto-optimal triples vary by dataset; heterogeneous CBA/CCA often balance quality and cost, while on PythonIO cheaper ABC equals expensive CCC at 99.21%.

The accountable protocol enables stage-level error origin plus repair/harm diagnosis, but accountability is not uniformly beneficial and is not a free accuracy intervention. Its demonstrated value is raising weak-pipeline performance and observability; strong pipelines generally match or only slightly exceed the best single model on constrained MCQs.
limitations: PythonIO, LogiQA, and AGIEval are discrete multiple-choice tasks whose agents emit one-letter answers, not open-ended software implementation, repository modification, test execution, requirements evolution, or an end-to-end SDLC.

No repeated generations, temperature/settings, statistical intervals/tests, or best-configuration selection correction are reported, so small best-single gaps and even large protocol deltas lack estimated stochastic uncertainty.

Structured accountability is confounded with changed prompts and handoff representation. Offline logging/blame alone cannot cause accuracy gains; the study does not isolate which protocol component produces them.

Blame assignment requires a ground-truth answer after every stage. The paper acknowledges that production systems need proxies such as executable unit tests, verifier agents, or self-consistency checks, whose accuracy and cost are not tested here.

Results use three proprietary models in one evaluation window; the paper inconsistently names model B as Claude 3.5 Sonnet in selection text and Claude Sonnet 4 in tables/pricing. Provider updates and pricing can change both rankings and Pareto fronts.

Several reported values conflict: LogiQA CCA is +3.76 in Table III but +6.99 in prose; Table III's best LogiQA value is CCC 85.16, while the Pareto discussion calls CCA 85.51. These errors weaken exact configuration conclusions.

There is no production deployment, user study, human-review workflow, security evaluation, failure injection, concurrency, or long-horizon state. Industrial-partner involvement and released logs do not substitute for operational evidence.
future_work: Replicate across open-source models and later model versions with fixed prompts, timestamps, repeated runs, paired tests, and confidence intervals.

Replace unavailable runtime gold labels with independently evaluated executable tests, multiple verifiers, self-consistency checks, or external validators and measure their own false repair/harm rates.
Extend from one-letter MCQs to open-ended repository-level software tasks and end-to-end SDLC workflows with production-like tools, state, failures, and security constraints.
Ablate logging, structured schemas, role instructions, and validation separately to identify which accountability component changes accuracy.
combinable_methods: Persist each stage's input, output, model/version, prompt, token/latency/cost metadata, and artifact delta; compute earliest unrepaired error origin plus repair and harm rates for regression diagnosis.
Use structured typed handoffs and explicit Planner-Executor-Critic responsibilities, but validate the handoff with an external signal rather than treating trace logging itself as verification.
Cast models by measured role aptitude or use confidence-aware routing: reliable planner, high-repair/low-harm executor, and critic selected for net repair rather than raw model rank.
Monitor both repair and harm so a critic that fixes some failures but corrupts correct artifacts cannot appear beneficial on repair count alone.
Select configurations on a task-specific accuracy-cost-latency Pareto frontier and retain the strongest monolithic model as a baseline and fallback.

quotes.text: We compare three inference regimes: (1) Single-model baselines. Each model answers end-to-end with the prompt above. These runs establish individual capability and serve as reference points.
quotes.use: Defines the monolithic reference condition.

quotes.text: On the PythonIO benchmark, the accuracy gains were even more substantial for several configurations. The BBB configuration's accuracy increased by 36.22 percentage points, from 61.42% to 97.64%. Similarly large gains were recorded for BAB (+33.07 points), CBA (+27.56 points), and CCA (+26.78 points).
quotes.use: Provides exact large accountable-versus-simple pipeline gains.

quotes.text: Finally, the Strong Accountable pipeline (representing the best of the CCC and CBA configurations) consistently performs at or near the level of the best monolithic model, and in the case of LogiQA, slightly surpasses it.
quotes.use: Qualifies the multi-agent result as mostly matching, rather than broadly beating, the best single model.

quotes.text: Claude Sonnet 4 (Model B) was the most effective Executor, achieving a repair rate of 10.01%, which was significantly higher than any other model in that role. It maintained a low harm rate of 0.25% as an Executor. In the Critic role, its repair rate was 3.04%, while its harm rate was the highest recorded for that role at 1.90%.
quotes.use: Quantifies role-specific repair and harm rather than aggregate accuracy alone.

quotes.text: Structured outputs and logging also add overhead: compared to simple monolithic baselines, accountable pipelines increased costs by about 2–3 × and raised median latency from ∼2s in lightweight settings to 20–25s in heavier ones (roughly 8–10 × slower).
